title: EU AI Office's power to fine model providers goes live — Article 101 arms the regulator with 3% penalties
subtitle: The Commission's year of paper-only oversight of general-purpose AI ends today, with fine authority up to 3% of global turnover or €15 million now available against every frontier lab that sells into the bloc.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The EU AI Office's penalty powers over providers of general-purpose AI models become applicable on August 2, unlocking fines of up to 3% of global annual turnover or €15 million — whichever is higher — under Article 101 of the AI Act. GPAI obligations themselves have been in force since August 2, 2025, but for the past twelve months the AI Office could only request documentation, publish guidance, and negotiate. Beginning today it can also open formal proceedings, demand corrective measures, restrict or withdraw a model from the EU market, and impose administrative fines against any general-purpose model placed on the market since last August — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI, Moonshot and every other frontier provider that has shipped into the bloc is now inside the enforcement perimeter.

The specific obligations the Office can now enforce sit in Articles 53 and 55 of the AI Act. Every GPAI provider owes technical documentation of the model, information for downstream deployers, a policy for respecting EU copyright, and a public summary of training data. Providers of models judged to present systemic risk — the tier defined by 10^25 FLOP of training compute plus market-share signals — carry additional duties: model evaluations aligned with the Commission's evaluation protocol, adversarial testing, serious incident reporting to the AI Office, and cybersecurity protections for model weights. Models placed on the market before August 2, 2025 receive a longer runway; enforcement against that legacy cohort does not start until August 2, 2027.

The Code of Practice for GPAI providers, published by the Commission in July 2025 and signed by most frontier labs during the fall, remains the primary compliance vehicle. Signing the Code is voluntary but creates a presumption of conformity with Article 53; providers that refused to sign now carry the burden of demonstrating equivalent measures on their own. The July version of the Code focuses on transparency, copyright, and safety-and-security practices for systemic-risk models, and it is the document the AI Office will most likely reach for first when it evaluates whether a given provider is meeting its duties. Fines under Article 101 top out at 3% of global turnover for procedural violations of GPAI rules; the higher 7%-of-turnover tier reserved for prohibited-practices breaches sits under a different article and applied on a different clock.

For learners: the interesting question over the next few quarters is not whether the AI Office issues a headline fine — that will take investigations that unfold over months — but which providers move first on documentation and evaluation disclosures, and which quietly resist. Watch for updated model cards, public evaluation summaries, and training-data manifests from the frontier labs in the coming weeks; the ones that treat today as a compliance milestone will tell you something about how they read the regulator, and the ones that don't will tell you the same thing in a different direction. This is the first serious test of whether an AI-specific regulator with real teeth can shape frontier-lab behavior without slowing capability development. Both possibilities are live.
